COVERT VIDEO SURVEILLANCE OF EMPLOYEES AND THE CALIFORNIA RIGHT OF PRIVACY (CAL. CONST., ART. I, § 1; LAB. CODE § 435; HERNANDEZ V. HILLSIDES, INC.; HILL V. NATIONAL COLLEGIATE ATHLETIC ASSN.; SHULMAN V. GROUP W PRODUCTIONS, INC.; SANDERS V. AMERICAN BROADCASTING COMPANIES) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about covert video surveillance of employees at work — the situation presented when recording or monitoring equipment is placed in a work area such as the shared second-floor office, used by employees including Jordan Lee, who holds the position of Administrative Coordinator.

It describes the text of the state constitutional privacy provision (California Constitution, article I, section 1); the three elements of a state constitutional privacy claim and the balancing of countervailing interests set out in Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. (1994) 7 Cal.4th 1; the two elements of the common law tort of intrusion into seclusion stated in Shulman v. Group W Productions, Inc. (1998) 18 Cal.4th 200; the holding in Sanders v. American Broadcasting Companies (1999) 20 Cal.4th 907 that workplace privacy is not an all-or-nothing characteristic; the California Supreme Court’s application of both frameworks to a hidden workplace camera in Hernandez v. Hillsides, Inc. (2009) 47 Cal.4th 272; and Labor Code section 435, which forbids audio or video recording of an employee in a restroom, locker room, or changing room.

This sheet describes what the authorities say. It does not evaluate any particular monitoring arrangement, does not determine whether any recording or observation is lawful, and does not predict how any court would resolve a dispute.

THE STATE CONSTITUTIONAL PRIVACY PROVISION IS ONE CLAUSE OF ARTICLE I, SECTION 1
California’s constitutional right of privacy is not a separate article or a dedicated section. It is a single word — “privacy” — at the end of the list of inalienable rights in article I, section 1 of the California Constitution. The section declares that all people are by nature free and independent and have inalienable rights, and then enumerates them: enjoying and defending life and liberty; acquiring, possessing, and protecting property; and pursuing and obtaining safety, happiness, and privacy.

The Legislative Counsel’s publication of the section records that it was added in its present form by Proposition 7 at the election of November 5, 1974. The California Supreme Court reproduced the same sentence when it construed the provision in Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn., adding italics of its own to the word “privacy” in the quoted passage.

A CONSTITUTIONAL PRIVACY CLAIM HAS THREE ELEMENTS
Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. set out what a plaintiff must establish to make out an invasion of the state constitutional right of privacy. The court framed it as three elements: a legally protected privacy interest; a reasonable expectation of privacy in the circumstances; and conduct by the defendant constituting a serious invasion of privacy.

The third element carries an express threshold. Hill explained that no community could function if every intrusion into the realm of private action, however slight or trivial, gave rise to a cause of action, and that an actionable invasion must be serious enough in its nature, scope, and actual or potential impact to amount to an egregious breach of the social norms underlying the privacy right.

COMPETING INTERESTS ARE WEIGHED, AND NO LEAST-OFFENSIVE-ALTERNATIVE BURDEN IS IMPOSED
Hill described the privacy right as one that is weighed rather than applied absolutely: privacy concerns are not absolute and must be balanced against other important interests.

Hill also declined to require a private organization, acting where expectations of privacy are already decreased, to justify its conduct as the least offensive alternative available. The court said it had been directed to no case imposing that burden and would not impose it. Hernandez v. Hillsides, Inc. repeated that point twenty-five years later and applied it to a private employer.

THE COMMON LAW TORT OF INTRUSION HAS TWO ELEMENTS
Alongside the constitutional provision, California recognizes the common law tort of intrusion into seclusion. Shulman v. Group W Productions, Inc. stated its two elements: intrusion into a private place, conversation or matter, and intrusion in a manner highly offensive to a reasonable person.

On the first element, Shulman said the plaintiff must show that the defendant penetrated some zone of physical or sensory privacy surrounding the plaintiff, or obtained unwanted access to data about the plaintiff. On the second, Shulman said that in the difficult cases — many of which involve hidden cameras and miniature recording equipment — California tort law provides no bright line, and each case must be taken on its facts.

PRIVACY AT WORK IS NOT AN ALL-OR-NOTHING CHARACTERISTIC
Sanders v. American Broadcasting Companies concerned a reporter who took a job alongside the plaintiff and secretly recorded workplace conversations with a camera hidden in her hat. The Court of Appeal had held that a worker whose conversations could be seen and heard by colleagues could not reasonably expect them to stay private. The California Supreme Court reversed.

Sanders held that privacy, for purposes of the intrusion tort, is not a binary, all-or-nothing characteristic; there are degrees and nuances to societal recognition of privacy expectations, and the fact that the privacy expected in a given setting is incomplete does not make the expectation unreasonable as a matter of law. The holding the court stated was a narrow one: the possibility of being overheard by coworkers does not, as a matter of law, make unreasonable an employee’s expectation that interactions within a nonpublic workplace will not be secretly videotaped by a journalist.

HERNANDEZ V. HILLSIDES APPLIES BOTH FRAMEWORKS THROUGH ONE TWO-PART INQUIRY
Hernandez v. Hillsides, Inc. is the California Supreme Court’s decision on covert video surveillance by an employer. Two clerical employees shared an enclosed office at a residential facility for abused children. The facility’s director, having learned that someone was using a computer in that office late at night to view pornographic websites, installed a hidden camera in the office without telling them.

The court restated the common law tort in the same two-element form as Shulman: intentional intrusion into a place, conversation, or matter as to which the plaintiff has a reasonable expectation of privacy, occurring in a manner highly offensive to a reasonable person. It described the second element as essentially a policy determination about whether the intrusion is highly offensive in the particular circumstances. Because the constitutional and common law standards largely parallel one another, the court analyzed both under a single two-part inquiry: the nature of any intrusion upon reasonable expectations of privacy, and the offensiveness or seriousness of the intrusion, including any justification and other relevant interests.

WORKPLACE PRIVACY EXPECTATIONS ARE DIMINISHED BUT NOT ABSENT
Hernandez began its analysis of the first element from the premise that privacy expectations may be significantly diminished in the workplace but are not lacking altogether.

The court identified the factors Sanders had linked to the reasonableness of a privacy expectation: the identity of the intruder; the extent to which other persons had access to the place in question and could see or hear the plaintiff; and the means by which the intrusion occurred. It then placed workplaces along a spectrum, with open and publicly accessible work areas at one end and areas reserved for bodily functions or inherently personal acts at the other, and located the shared office before it between those extremes.

A SHARED, ENCLOSED OFFICE CAN SUPPORT A REASONABLE EXPECTATION OF PRIVACY
Applying those factors, Hernandez concluded that a jury could find the required intrusion. The court pointed to the physical setting: an enclosed office with a door that could be shut and locked and window blinds that could be drawn, which allowed the occupants some measure of refuge and escape from visual and aural interruption, including interruption by their employer.

Shared occupancy and third-party access did not defeat the expectation. The court said privacy is not wholly lacking because the occupants of an office can see one another, or because colleagues, supervisors, visitors, and security and maintenance personnel have varying degrees of access. It concluded that the plaintiffs had no reasonable expectation that their employer would intrude so tangibly into their semiprivate office.

ADVANCE NOTICE AND CONSENT BEAR ON THE ANALYSIS
Hernandez treated notice and consent as part of the first element. Citing Hill, the court noted that notice of and consent to an impending intrusion can inhibit reasonable expectations of privacy and can limit the intrusion upon personal dignity by giving people an opportunity to regulate their conduct while monitored. On the record before it, the court found the plaintiffs could not plausibly be said to have received warning of the surveillance or to have agreed to it in advance.

The closing paragraphs return to the same point from the other direction. The court said that nothing in its opinion was meant to encourage such surveillance measures, particularly in the absence of adequate notice to persons within camera range that their actions may be viewed and taped.
